justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline view on the underlying asset, with prices drifting slightly higher from the current level near 219–220. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the last observed price, expecting minimal drift and relying primarily on mean-reversion tendencies over very short windows. The one-week estimate of 221 incorporates a small upward bias consistent with a mild positive trend, while the one-month estimate of 224 extrapolates that trend further, assuming no major regime change. The incremental increases across horizons are intentionally modest, reflecting the reality that short-term price forecasting has limited directional edge beyond momentum persistence.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is a direct reflection of how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 11 points, capturing typical intraday-to-overnight volatility. By one week, the interval expands to 24 points, incorporating the possibility of a meaningful macro or sector-specific catalyst shifting sentiment. At one month, the 48-point range acknowledges that a wide range of outcomes is plausible — earnings reports, Federal Reserve communications, geopolitical developments, and shifts in risk appetite can all accumulate over four weeks to produce substantially different outcomes than the baseline.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes well outside even my stated intervals. On the downside, a surprise deterioration in macroeconomic data — particularly inflation re-acceleration prompting a hawkish Fed pivot, or a sudden credit event — could produce sharp selling pressure that breaks below the lower bound of my one-month interval. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected earnings cycle, a ceasefire or geopolitical de-escalation, or a dovish policy surprise could drive a breakout rally that exceeds 248.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume roughly stable volatility conditions. If realized volatility were to spike — as happens during liquidity crises or flash crashes — all three intervals could be simultaneously violated. Tail risks are by definition underweighted in probabilistic forecasts built around central tendency assumptions, so these numbers should be treated as reasonable baseline expectations rather than hard bounds on what is possible.
